findings.title: Stone and iron as a material limit case
findings.claim: The stone-or-iron state functions as a limit-case in the wider new-creation exchange: resistant matter sharpens the counterchallenge without setting creation's boundary.
findings.mechanism: The focus commands a spoken answer and asks its addressees to imagine being stone or iron. Supplied later objections about bones, fragments, and new creation (17:98 and 32:10) meet the focus's material alternatives; 17:99, 30:27, and 50:15 supply first-creation and renewed-creation language. Their contact makes the hard materials a test of whether any material state can bound re-creation. The legacy reader-walk account of 17:49, 17:51, and 17:52 adds a movement from remains through first origination to summons-response, but remains attributed context.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader sees why the reply names unusually resistant matter: it pushes the imagined obstacle to its limit and keeps even that limit within the reach of origination.
findings.containment: The focus still tells its addressees to imagine becoming stone or iron; the restriction and boundary branches are contextual images, not lexical substitutes for either noun. The imperative does not itself change matter. The 17:49/51/52 sequence is legacy-unbound, and the connected wider ayat supply Arabic surfaces without target morphology.

epistemic.reason: A trusted cross-run finding anchors both focus materials and the limit-case claim. Exact Arabic in the supplied 17:98/99, 30:27, 32:10, and 50:15 connections supports the wider creation relation, but connection rows are nominations and lack target morphology; the additional pericope sequence comes from legacy-unbound reader walks.

findings.title: Stone that can yield
findings.claim: A wider stone image holds hardness together with yielding: the same material that makes a limit-case in 17:50 can split, release water, and descend in another supplied context.
findings.mechanism: The focus's stone carrier meets 2:74, whose exact Arabic first compares hearts to stones and then describes stones that release rivers, split to let water emerge, or descend from awe. That contact shifts stone from an image of unresponsive resistance to hard matter that can also yield or respond.
findings.reader_payoff: Hardness no longer has to mean inertness; the reader can keep the material force of stone while seeing its other supplied behavior remain live.
findings.containment: The two passages do not identify the same stones or establish a direct allusion. The yielding image does not cancel the focus's material challenge or make every stone fluid or responsive.

epistemic.reason: The connection packet supplies the exact 2:74 Arabic, but not its target morphology or lexical analysis; the relation is reassessed from the surface and remains a bounded contextual reading.

findings.title: Iron as boundary and workable matter
findings.claim: Wider iron images keep its hardness intact while showing iron worked into a boundary and softened by action.
findings.mechanism: The focus's iron carrier meets 18:96, where iron pieces are fitted between two slopes and heated into a structure, and 34:10, whose supplied Arabic says iron was softened for David. The first contact makes iron a boundary material; the second shows that its resistance is not immutability. Together they add a workable-material reading to the focus's hard iron without turning it into the same scene.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can distinguish iron's real toughness from an absolute inability to be shaped or softened.
findings.containment: These are separate contextual images, not evidence that 17:50 directly alludes to either passage. Neither shaping nor softening establishes resurrection, and the target morphology for both connected ayat is absent.

epistemic.reason: Exact target Arabic is supplied for both connections, but their source directions are nominations and target morphology is absent. The 34:10 top-level note reads the softening as counterevidence while its reciprocal source note records a no-value judgment, so the relation remains qualified rather than inherited as a verdict.

findings.title: A mirrored impossible demand
findings.claim: The focus's stone challenge can be read beside the reported later demand for the sky to fall in pieces as two attempts to make an impossible state concrete and manipulable.
findings.mechanism: The focus's stone carrier supplies hard, fragmentable matter; the retrospective support reports that 17:92 asks for the sky itself to fall in detached pieces. Their contact shifts the focus's material challenge into a scale-changing echo, from imagined bodily matter to the sky.
findings.reader_payoff: The reported echo makes the challenge's scale visible: the focus tests the body's hardest imagined form, while the later demand turns the sky itself into the object of an impossible test.
findings.containment: This remains an attributed analogy from one legacy-unbound retrospective note. The packet supplies no 17:92 Arabic surface or typed anchor, so no direct lexical echo, intentional reference, or settled sequence is claimed.

epistemic.reason: The candidate supplies a concrete reported trigger and a possible scale-shifting relation, but the target Arabic and any independent context anchor are absent; retain the analogy only with that uncertainty explicit.
